new_statements.rule_in_words: In morphologically simple words main stress falls on the penultimate syllable (Hannß, citing Uhle 1894). Under affixation the archival data show only tendencies: stress may stay on the old penult, shift to the new penult, or the word may carry double/triple stress; final stress is exceptional and emphatic; verbal stress is too variable to state rules. Hannß therefore treats penultimate stress as a tendency rather than an exceptionless rule (p. 3: 'a tendency to place stress on the penultimate syllable, although this is not compulsory') and does not mark stress elsewhere in the grammar (p. 123).
new_statements.secondary_stress: No secondary stress as such; Hannß describes 'double' and 'triple' stress: a monosyllabic nominal stem plus a bisyllabic suffix receives double stress (e.g. hux'-kama), most trisyllabic nominal stems already bear alternating double stress with the first syllable stressed (p. 119), and verbs optionally take a second stress on the 1sg markers -u/-a or in-group -acu (p. 121).
new_statements.exceptions: Bisyllabic stem + bisyllabic suffix and mono-/bisyllabic verbs with 1sg -u/-a (p. 3); monosyllabic stem + monosyllabic suffix keeps stress in situ, so it is often not the penult (p. 118); monosyllabic verb stems with a monosyllabic suffix tend to shift stress to the final syllable, e.g. imperative ondí (p. 122); stress on the final syllable is exceptional and emphatic; declarative -cay is always unstressed (p. 120); purposive -srap'a keeps stress on its own first syllable (p. 122-123); stress marking is inconsistent within sources and Polo (1901) and Métraux (1935) mark no stress at all (p. 117).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in a dormant language reconstructed from archival transcriptions (Uhle 1894, Polo 1901, Lehmann 1929, Métraux 1935, Vellard 1949-1967), not from fieldwork; examples are cited forms and text words from those sources; Hannß calls the patterns tendencies, not rules.
new_statements.identity_note: Hannß 2008 describes Uchumataqu, the Uru of Irohito (Iru-Itu / Ancoaqui) on the Desaguadero, Bolivia, as recorded 1894-1952; Glottolog lists Uchumataqu, Iro-Itu and Uro as alternate names of uruu1244, so the identity matches. It is not Chipaya (chip1262), and it is distinct from the Uru of Ch'imu / Puno bay (Peru) treated by Hannß 2014 and Cerrón-Palomino et al. 2016, which Glottolog also files under uruu1244. Hannß's stress data come from archival transcriptions (chiefly Vellard 1949-67, Uhle 1894, Lehmann 1929), not fieldwork, and she calls the penultimate pattern a tendency with many exceptions under affixation.
